text: Singapore's National Symbols Were All Written on a Deadline
Singapore's national anthem was not written for a nation.
It was written for the reopening of a concert hall.

That anthem, along with the flag flown outside every void deck and the pledge recited by every schoolchild, exists because two different governments needed something to point to on a tight deadline: once in 1959, when self-government arrived faster than anyone had planned for, and again in 1966, when a newly independent country was still absorbing the shock of race riots and an unwanted divorce from Malaysia.
The flag came first, and it came from a standing start.

When Britain granted Singapore self-government in 1959, the Union Jack that had flown over the island for nearly 140 years suddenly needed replacing, and Deputy Prime Minister Toh Chin Chye was put in charge of finding something to replace it with.
He studied the flags of every country represented at the United Nations to make sure Singapore's wouldn't be confused with anyone else's, then brought designs to cabinet.
His own suggestion, a plain red field, was rejected outright: ministers worried it would read as a communist banner.
An early version with three stars was scrapped for a similar reason, since three stars too closely echoed the flag of the Malayan Communist Party.

What survived the process was a compromise between two communities: red and white stripes, a crescent moon to reassure Malay Singaporeans this wasn't going to be a Chinese state, and five stars, standing for democracy, peace, progress, justice and equality, to satisfy a Chinese majority that wanted something closer to the constellation on China's own flag.
The whole process, from first sketch to public unveiling, took barely two months.
The anthem's path there was stranger still.

In 1958, more than a year before self-government existed as a political fact, the Municipal Council needed a rousing number to close the reopening ceremony for the newly renovated Victoria Theatre, and commissioned the composer Zubir Saeed to write one around the council's own motto, Majulah Singapura, "Onward Singapore."
Zubir took two weeks.
He later recalled the difficulty of the assignment: a melody short enough to be singable, with words simple enough that every race in Singapore could understand them.
The song premiered at the theatre's reopening concert on the 6th of September 1958, a piece of civic pageantry with no wider ambition attached to it.
It was only the following year, once Toh Chin Chye went looking for something to serve as the new state's anthem, that someone remembered the council's old commissioned tune and handed it to him.

Majulah Singapura was introduced to the public as Singapore's national anthem on the 3rd of December 1959, the same day the flag was unveiled, at the installation of Yusof bin Ishak as the country's first Malayan-born head of state.
The pledge took longer to arrive, and it was born out of something considerably darker than a concert hall reopening.
Singapore was expelled from Malaysia in August 1965, still carrying the memory of race riots the year before that had killed 23 people and injured hundreds more.
Two months after independence, the idea of a formal pledge began circulating in government, and the task of writing it fell to Foreign Minister S.
Rajaratnam.
Through three drafts over several months, he kept returning to one idea: that a country this fractured needed to name its divisions before it could claim to rise above them.
An early version asked citizens to "forget differences of race, language and religion."

Rajaratnam revised it to something more honest about what was actually possible, a pledge to build a nation "regardless of race, language or religion" rather than pretending those differences could simply be forgotten.

Translated into Chinese, Malay and Tamil, the pledge was recited for the first time on the 24th of August 1966, by roughly 500,000 students across 529 schools, standing with their right hands raised toward the flag in a gesture that would later be replaced by today's clenched fist over the heart.
None of this is how national symbols are supposed to come together.

Anthems are meant to accrue meaning over generations; flags are meant to descend from old battles and older loyalties; pledges, where they exist at all, tend to arrive fully formed at a founding moment rather than being drafted three times by a Foreign Minister two months after the country's neighbours had told it to leave.

Singapore's version of all three happened in a hurry, under duress, designed by a handful of people who were mostly trying to solve an immediate political problem rather than write something for the ages.

Why it matters today: the flag, anthem and pledge are recited and saluted so often that they can feel like they have always simply existed, the way older nations treat symbols inherited from centuries they never had to live through.

Singapore's were assembled under real time pressure by specific, namable people who had weeks or months rather than generations to get them right, which makes their survival, largely unchanged, into the present the more interesting fact.
